# Draft:Australian Indigenous smoking ceremonies

----
Australian Indigenous smoking ceremonies are traditional cultural practices conducted by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia. We know Aboriginal Australians have been active on Australia around 65,000 years and that they have practiced Smoking Ceremonies long before colonisation. Smoking ceremonies are used for spiritual cleansing, healing, and ceremonial purposes. The ceremonies are intended to purify people and places, promote wellbeing, and strengthen connections to Country, community, and ancestral heritage.
Smoking ceremonies are commonly associated with protection from harmful spiritual influences believed to inhabit the land and waters. They are regarded in many Aboriginal cultures as an important means of establishing or reaffirming relationships between individuals, community, and Country.
Ritual cleansing through smoke is not unique to Australia; comparable practices involving the burning of plant materials for spiritual or medicinal purposes occur in various cultures worldwide. For example, some Native American groups use white sage in purification rituals. Within Aboriginal Australian traditions, a range of native plants are used depending on regional availability and cultural protocols.
One plant frequently associated with smoking practices is Eremophila longifolia, commonly known as emu bush. The leaves are placed on hot embers to produce smoke, which is directed over individuals or spaces. Scientific studies have identified antibacterial, antifungal, and antioxidant properties in this species, supporting its traditional medicinal use. Smoking with emu bush has been used for healing, illness prevention.
Other plants used in smoking ceremonies and for medicinal purposes include native peppermint Agonis flexuosa, cauliflower bush Cassinia longifolia, sandalwood Santalum spicatum, and various species of eucalyptus, tea tree, and paperbark. The specific plants and methods vary among different Aboriginal Nations and language groups.
Smoking ceremonies are performed for a range of purposes, including funerals, celebrations, healing rituals, and community gatherings. They may also serve as a gesture of goodwill or welcome. In many communities, conducting a ceremony for others is considered an act of respect and cultural responsibility.
The ceremony itself typically involves placing plant material on embers to create smoke, which is then guided over participants, objects, or areas using branches or by hand. Participants may draw the smoke toward themselves as a symbolic act of cleansing or protection. There are different types of smoking practices with different uses, and ceremonies are conducted according to local cultural knowledge and authority.
In contemporary Australia, smoking ceremonies are sometimes incorporated into public events, educational programs, and official gatherings. When conducted by appropriate cultural custodians, these ceremonies are intended to acknowledge Indigenous traditions and maintain the cultural and spiritual significance of the practice.
Not all Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander communities perform smoking ceremonies, and practices differ significantly between Nations. The observance of local protocols and engagement with Traditional Custodians are considered essential to maintaining cultural integrity.
